summary: This clipped Ecological Monographs article (Taylor et al., 2014) reports the first exhaustive molecular census of soil fungi in a boreal black spruce ecosystem near Fairbanks, Alaska. Using ITS sequencing of 28,884 clones from 12 sites, the authors recorded 1002 fungal OTUs and estimated a fungus:plant ratio of at least 17:1, which extrapolates globally to about 6 million species. They also report that closely related fungi often occupy divergent niches, suggesting deterministic niche partitioning. The note is truncated mid-results.
one_line: Molecular census of soil fungi in Alaskan black spruce forest finds 1002 OTUs, a stable 17:1 fungus-to-plant ratio, and niche partitioning among related fungi.
key_facts: The study was published in Ecological Monographs with first publication date 01 February 2014.
The authors are D. Lee Taylor, Teresa N. Hollingsworth, Jack W. McFarland, Niall J. Lennon, Chad Nusbaum, and Roger W. Ruess.
The census recorded 1002 fungal taxa (OTUs) in black spruce forest soils of interior Alaska.
The fungus:plant ratio in Picea mariana forest soils from interior Alaska is at least 17:1 and is regionally stable.
A global extrapolation of the ratio would suggest 6 million fungal species, versus leading estimates ranging from 616 000 to 1.5 million.
The study concludes that 98% of fungi remain undescribed and that many of these species occupy unique niches.
Hawksworth (1991) estimated a ratio of roughly 6 to 1 of fungi to vascular plants in the UK, yielding a global extrapolation of 1.5 million species.
The study sampled 12 of the 151 black spruce sites studied by Hollingsworth et al. (2006, 2008), with 48 samples from organic and mineral horizons.
Soil samples were collected as 50 cores per site, 1.8 cm in diameter by 20 cm deep, along four parallel transects.
Rarefaction analysis reached saturation, and 117 of the 1002 OTUs were singletons.
Of 97 plant species documented at the 12 sites, 60 are vascular, giving the approximately 17:1 multiplier.
The mean F:P ratio across sites was 16.0 (±6.1 SD), and the rarefied ratio was essentially constant at 16.8 with eight or more sites.
Clones were clustered into OTUs at 97% sequence identity across the ITS region using the Cap3 program.
Black spruce (Picea mariana) forests cover about 40% of the Alaskan landscape, roughly 40% of forested land in Alaska per the introduction.
Phylogenetic analyses focused on three genus-level clusters: Cortinarius (Basidiomycota), Leptodontidium (Ascomycota), and Mortierella (former Zygomycota).
